I say: Ibn Arabi draws our attention to how much subtler God's self-disclosures are than the image that puzzles the mind and defeats our understanding. We can become so confused that we even ask whether the image we see is real. The mind cannot say it is sheer nothingness, because it knows that it is not nothing; but it cannot say it is pure existence either, because it knows that the image is not a separate thing, distinct from what it reflects, nor is it pure possibility.

The mirror and the image it shows are meant to guide us toward understanding how God's light passes through things, how He appears in the mirrors of natures, and how He appears in each thing according to what it can receive. A possible thing's existence is not identical with its nature—what it is. Nor is it identical with God's own existence, which depends on nothing, since the possible thing is limited, incomplete, and dependent. Yet it is not wholly separate from God, because it cannot exist on its own, as we have already proved.

We have also shown that God's self-disclosure to things is one, and that He gives existence in one way. Its many forms come from the many natures and their differences. The same mirror does not receive a repeated act of self-disclosure. This shows that knowing a reality requires that the reality itself be present, not a second image of it. If the image's appearance were the same as the reality's own appearance, God's self-disclosure would be repeated. The people of spiritual insight have already shown why this cannot be.

Another subtle point now becomes clear. Philosophers disagree about how the human soul knows the truths of things when it is freed from the body and joined to the source that gives existence. Does it know by receiving forms from that source, or in the opposite way—by seeing those truths within the active source itself? Both views have been defended in books on the subject. But careful reflection shows that the answer is neither. The soul becomes fully joined to its source by letting its own sense of self fall away and finding its life in the Real. Absorbed in seeing God, it sees things as they truly are in the world. It does not see a second copy of these realities, different from the things themselves. That would mean God's self-revelation had been repeated, which we have already shown cannot happen.

The mystics and the Stoic philosophers also rejected the idea that knowledge is only a mental image. They say that things exist in the world just as they are known to God; their existence comes from Him, not from themselves. God's knowing things is the same as His giving them existence through the light of His being. So when a person with direct insight sees the forms of things through contact with the sacred world, that person sees the realities themselves as they exist—not copies or likenesses of them. Someone with limited understanding, however, sees God through the mirror of things and forms a belief about Him from what they see. God appears to that person in a form that matches their belief. If, on the Day of Resurrection, He appears in a different form, that person rejects Him and seeks refuge from Him.

This is why people's beliefs differ: each person sees God through different things. It is what is meant by God's words, “I am as My servant thinks of Me.” Each person accepts the ways God appears that fit their condition and rejects what their nature cannot receive.

The traveler who has reached God and let go of the self sees Him without anything created standing between them. But this state can also keep the traveler from seeing created things: absorbed in God, the traveler is too narrowly focused to see anything else. Before letting go of the self, created things hide God. Afterward, the traveler may lose sight of God's different levels and the ways He appears through His names and qualities.

The person who knows God fully returns from this unity to the many details, guided by what they have seen in unity. They see God through His names and qualities, and see creation through God. They travel through the world of realities, lit by their Lord. At this level, they know things by knowing their source: the source of their existence, the source through which they appear, and the source of their natures and fixed identities. They can then truly say they see things as they are, in God's noble face, which holds the secrets of the heavens and the earth.

Every mirror other than God Himself reflects something because, considered by itself, it is empty of the images and qualities it shows. This is true of natures that reflect existence; of the universal imagination, which displays the world of images; of a person's imagination, which displays imagined forms; and of ice, water, crystal, and iron, which display visible images. Hearing, taste, smell, and touch also display the things they sense.

But their ability to reflect is not the same as their own nature or existence: each mirror exists in its own particular way. So what we see in a mirror is not wholly the same as the thing itself, but neither is it wholly different from it. If you focus on the mirror itself—on its being made of iron or glass, for example—it blocks your view of the image. Its particular nature takes over, and it no longer shows the image as before.

If you stop looking at the iron or glass as a thing in itself and instead notice how it is connected to the image, you see the image across from you. The mirror remains what it is, even when you do not pay attention to it. So what you see is not simply the same as the thing's own existence. The mirror's particular nature hides the thing's true existence in the way that nature allows. This is why images look different in different mirrors—larger or smaller, straight or bent, clear or faint—because their surfaces may be curved, hollowed, polished, or cloudy, even when we do not notice these features. The same is true of all other possible mirrors.

God is different. His essence gives rise to things and to our understanding of them. His essence is the mirror through which things appear just as they are. His essence, by itself and without any added quality, is the source of things; so seeing His essence is the source of seeing things. Full knowledge of a complete cause gives full knowledge of its effect. God knows Himself only through Himself: His essence and His awareness of it are one, without any difference or division. These are also the source of the world and of our awareness of it. In the same way, we can know created things only through their own existence. Their existence and their being known are not two separate things. Because cause and effect are joined without a gap, the existence of created things and our awareness of them are joined in the same way. Just as the existence of things depends on God, so does our knowledge of them as they truly are.
God's essence, then, is the mirror through which all things, general and particular, are known as they really are, without error or falsehood—unlike the mirrors of possible beings.

A consequence: We cannot truly know any thing without knowing the one who brings it into being, as we have already explained. Each thing has one way of existing, and that existence comes from one source. This follows from what we know about the impossibility of one thing's appearing twice and the oneness of God's self-revelation. It also shows why the philosophers are right to say that certain knowledge of things with causes comes only through knowing their causes. Think carefully about this, if you want to understand it fully.

A further point: You can now understand a familiar claim in general philosophy: knowing a particular cause gives you knowledge of its particular effect, while knowing a particular effect gives you knowledge only of its cause in general, not of that cause in its full detail. The usual explanation is that a particular cause produces a particular effect, while a particular effect calls for a cause of some kind. But that is only a claim, not a proof. The real reason is that an effect is a particular form of its cause, a specific way the cause appears. If you know the cause itself, you know its different forms and ways of acting. If you know only the effect, you know the cause only through that one form. It is like seeing a person's face in a mirror that makes it look larger or smaller, bent or straight.

Ibn Arabi explains this point in the chapter on Seth in The Bezels of Wisdom. He writes: “God's self-revelation always takes the form that the one receiving it is ready for. The one who receives it sees only their own image in the mirror of the Real; they do not see God Himself. Yet they know that their image appears only in Him. It is like an ordinary mirror: when you see images in it, you do not see the mirror, though you know that you see those images only in it.

“If you understand this, you have reached the highest point a human being can reach. Do not strain to rise higher: there is nothing beyond this, only sheer nothingness. God is your mirror when you see yourself, and you are His mirror when you see His names and how they take effect. Those names are not other than His essence.”

A further point: You can now see that people's different beliefs about God come from the different ways they see Him appear. People reject what they cannot accept from their own point of view. When God appears to pure intellects through statements about what He is not—He is not a body, He is not limited, and so on—those intellects accept this and declare Him free of likeness, imperfection, bodily form, and multiplicity. This is the way of minds that rise above the body, including some philosophers. Minds still tied to matter, such as imagination and the powers of embodied souls, reject this view. The same is true of people whose judgment is ruled by those powers, such as many literalists and those who picture God in human form: they can understand God only by comparing Him to created things.

When God appears through qualities that describe what He is—knowing, powerful, and so on—hearts and thinking souls accept Him. They are connected to bodies, yet their inner nature can also rise above them. Pure intellects, however, reject this way of speaking, because their nature allows them only to turn away from bodily things. Each kind of soul accepts the forms of God's appearance that suit it and rejects the ones it cannot receive. Everyone sees God only through their own way of existing and knows Him through their own identity. God appears to each person only in the mirror of that person's self.

Every power is hidden from God by its own limits and thinks nothing is better than itself. The angels argued over Adam; reason and imagination each claim mastery and refuse to yield to the other. Reason claims that it can grasp the truths of things through thought, but in fact thought gives it only mental ideas and the features that follow from things' existence—not the things as they are in the world. At its highest, while it relies on thought alone, reason knows in a general way that it has a Lord, free of defects and worldly qualities. But it does not directly see God, His self-revelation, or the detailed ways His light reaches every part of the worlds.

Imagination also claims rule and rejects reason's claims whenever they go beyond its own range, because it grasps meanings tied to particular things. Each power, then, has something of the devil's pride. Likewise, everyone apart from the fully developed human being has some share of hidden or open idolatry: they serve one of God's names, but not God through all His names. This is what the Qur'an says: “Some people worship God on the edge: if good comes to them, they are content; but if a trial comes, they turn away.”

The fully developed person accepts the Real, follows His light through all the ways He appears, and serves Him through all His names. Such a person is truly God's servant. That is why this is the fullest kind of human being. They see the First Reality through every divine and created appearance, without dividing God's essence or His act of appearing. As we have said, God's self-revelation is one. Its many forms come from the many ways He relates to things and the different conditions under which He appears; these are called natures and fixed identities.

These natures have no existence of their own and are not separately created or acted upon. They are joined in some way to the different forms of existence, which are shadows of the one light and flows of God's self-sustaining existence. Their features can then be said of them. Those who are complete know realities without doubt. They are servants of the All-Merciful, who walk humbly through the world of truth. When the ignorant speak to them, they answer, “Peace.” The ignorant are weak and limited in mind, unable to understand God's appearances in every place and at every level.

Defiant and rebellious souls, by contrast, do not honor what is sacred to God. They are far from Him and shut out from His light. They accept only what their own nature shows them. Of them, the Qur'an says, “You and what you worship apart from God are fuel for Hell.” Here, Hell means being shut out from seeing God's self-revelation and His nearness. These people mistake the many forms of existence—which are gifts from God and ways He appears—for separate things with their own power. They worship those things and credit them with creating what happens at lower levels, instead of worshipping God through all levels and all His names. They do not understand that God appears in every thing and is also beyond every thing. Glory to the One who is free of evil; glory to the One whose kingdom contains nothing that He does not will.

A brief summary: Traveler on the path of truth, look at unity and multiplicity, together and apart. If you see only unity, you are with God alone, and the multiplicity that belongs to creation disappears. If you see only multiplicity, you are with creation alone. But if you see unity hidden within multiplicity and multiplicity lost within unity, you have joined both kinds of perfection and reached the best of both states. Praise be to God, Lord of greatness and majesty, whose are the most beautiful names.
Chapter 34 — Another Proof That the Necessary Being Is One
The Necessary Being is complete in reality; nothing lies outside Him.

Know that the Necessary Being is utterly simple in reality. Anything whose reality is simple in this way is all things. So the Necessary Being is all things, and nothing is outside Him. Here is the general proof. Suppose some thing lay outside His reality. Then His very essence would make it true to say, “He is not that thing.” If His essence did not make this denial true, we would have to say, “It is not true that He is not that thing.” Since these are opposites, one must be true. Denying the denial means affirming the thing, so that thing would be part of His reality after all. But we assumed that it was not. That is impossible.

And if His essence makes it true that some thing is not Him, then His reality must include both what it is and the absence of that other thing. It would be made up of parts, at least in the mind's analysis. But we began by saying that His reality is simple. This, too, is impossible.

Here is the detailed proof. Suppose we say, “A human being is not a horse.” The reason for denying that a human is a horse must come from something other than humanity itself. A human, simply as a human, is human and nothing else. Humanity itself cannot be what makes a person “not a horse.” Otherwise, understanding what a human is would be the same as understanding “not a horse.” Anyone who understood humanity would also have to understand that contrast. But that is not what happens: we often understand what a human being is without thinking about horses. Still, in reality a human being is not a horse. That truth does not come from the idea of humanity alone. Considered simply as an idea, a human being is only human.

The same is true of every nature: considered on its own, each is only itself. But in reality a thing must also be either some other thing or not that thing. A human is either a horse or not a horse, a star or not a star. A star, in turn, is either human or not human. If a thing cannot be something else, then the denial of that other thing must apply to it. So in reality a human is made up of its humanity and the fact that it is not a horse, not a star, and not many other things. Its nature includes both what it is and these absences.

Anything to which a true denial applies must be made up of parts. In thought, you can picture the thing and what is being denied of it, compare them, and say that one does not belong to the other. What makes a thing what it is differs from what makes the denial true of it. If you say, “Zayd is not a writer,” the image of Zayd by itself cannot make the statement true. Otherwise, Zayd, simply as Zayd, would be nothing at all. The statement must include Zayd and some lack that means writing is absent from him, such as a lack of ability or readiness, or some other limit.

Pure action has no potential waiting to be fulfilled. Pure perfection has no readiness waiting to be realized. Absolute necessity and completeness leave no room for possibility, defect, or lack. Absolute existence has no trace of nonexistence in it. Otherwise, at least in the mind, it would combine action and potential, perfection and lack. The Necessary Being is existence itself, existing through Himself, without any trace of multiplicity or possibility. Nothing real is denied of Him; only negations, nonexistence, defects, and possibilities are denied of Him, because these are all forms of lack.

To deny lack is to affirm existence. So He is the fullness of all things, the completion of everything incomplete, and the one who makes up for every flaw, hardship, and defect. What is absent from Him is only the weakness, limits, and evil found in things. He is the goodness within all good things and the fullness of all existence. A thing is more fully and truly itself when complete than when it is incomplete. This is what the Qur'an points to when it says, “You did not throw when you threw; rather, God threw”; “He is with you wherever you are”; and “He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, and He knows all things.”
Chapter 35 — Why possibility and potential are not direct causes of existence

First, possibility is a kind of nonexistence, as we have already explained. What does not exist cannot cause or bring about anything. So possibility cannot be a cause, or even part of one. A cause brings something into existence. To do that, it must have a definite character that makes it the cause of this thing rather than another. Otherwise, there would be no more reason to call it a cause than to call something else a cause. Anything with a definite character in itself exists. So every cause exists, and anything that does not exist cannot be a cause.

This also shows that possibility cannot be part of a cause. If it were, it would have to play a causal role in making that cause effective, which brings us back to the same point. Whether we count possibility or leave it out makes no difference. Like countless other forms of nonexistence, it may be tied to the acting cause without producing its effect.

Here is a second proof. Possibilities in possible things must either differ only in number or differ in kind. If they differ only in number, then the possibility of one thing cannot cause another thing to exist. Things of the same kind share the same features that belong to them by their nature. So one possibility would have no greater claim to produce an effect than another. If one did produce that effect, they all would. For example, if the possibility of an agent's existence caused a heavenly sphere to exist, then the possibility belonging to every existing thing would produce a sphere. Each sphere would produce another, without end.

The other option—that possibilities differ in kind—does not hold either. Possibility is the opposite of necessity, and necessity is one. The opposite of one thing is one thing. Yet possibility can be divided into the possibility of a substance and the possibility of a quality. The possibility of a substance can then be divided into the possibility of a body and that of something without a body. What is divided must have something in common. And what we understand by possibility is the same in every case; the differences lie outside the idea of possibility itself. This makes possibility one kind of thing, with differences that come from other features. Besides, possibility is a kind of nonexistence, and nonexistence has no differences in itself. So possibility cannot bring anything into existence, whether its own subject or something else.

There is another proof. If possibility caused something, it would do so either with its subject or without it. If it acted without its subject, it would be independent of the subject in its action. But anything that acts independently of something also exists independently of it. Possibility would then be a separate substance, which is impossible. If possibility acted together with its subject, it would be part of the cause. A part of the cause would help make the whole cause effective. That effect—making the cause effective—would itself happen either with the subject or without it. The second option is impossible for the reason just given. The first would mean that this same possibility had to be part of the cause that makes it effective. We could repeat the question without end. This would create an endless chain of causes acting together, which is impossible.

You may ask how philosophers can say that the possibility of the First Intellect gives rise to the heavenly sphere, and that the possibilities of the other intellects give rise to the heavenly bodies. This gave their opponents a chance to mock them. One critic wrote that the claim that the First Intellect's possibility causes the outermost sphere, while its necessity causes the second intellect, was nonsense unfit even for ordinary people, let alone for anyone who claims to seek the truth.

I reply that saying “possibility causes something” means something like saying, “The absence of a cause causes the absence of its effect.” We do not mean that nonexistence acts in the world. We mean that when a cause is absent, its effect does not exist. In the same way, when philosophers say that possibility gives rise to a sphere, they mean that the First Intellect's existence has a possible limit, so what comes from it is a limited being, such as a body. In truth, existence causes existence, and nonexistence leads to nonexistence in the sense just explained. Nonexistence is not, in itself, a cause of something that exists; it can only play an indirect role.

The same applies to the possibility of an essence and to the possibilities that prepare matter to receive a form. They do not bring things into existence, whether those things are created outright or come into being through change. We have already shown that possibility itself causes nothing. As for the powers that prepare matter, if they acted without bodily matter taking part, they would be independent of matter in their action and would exist without matter.

As we have seen, anything independent of something in its action is independent of it in its existence too, since existence is part of the ability to act. That would make these powers immaterial, contrary to what we have assumed. If matter took part in their action, it would be receiving and being affected. Matter receives; it does not act or bring things about. A thing cannot be both necessary and possible in relation to the same thing, so matter cannot be the agent or a partner in bringing something about. Thus bodily powers, even when they are active, cannot give existence; how much less can powers that only prepare matter do so.

When philosophers say that the possibility of an essence causes it to exist, they mean only this: necessity and impossibility make a thing unable to receive the effect of a cause, while possibility does not. Possibility removes a barrier to the cause's action. It makes an essence able to receive existence, but does not itself bring existence about.

When they say that near and distant possibilities cause existence, they mean that they prepare matter to receive a form. In the world of matter and readiness, opposing forms get in the way of one another. When matter takes on one form, it cannot receive certain others. Some forms block a new form more strongly than others. Matter in the form of water is far from receiving the form of fire. Matter in the form of air is closer to receiving it. The hotter the air becomes, the more suited it is to fire. At a certain point it is equally open to either form. If it grows hotter still, its readiness to receive fire becomes stronger than its readiness to remain air. It then receives the fiery form and becomes fire.

So the possibility that comes with readiness means that a barrier or opposing form has been removed, either entirely or in part. When the barrier is entirely gone, the potential is near; when it is only partly gone, the potential is distant. A body's balance of qualities, though it is itself a real quality we can feel, can be called a readiness for the forms of animal, plant, or mineral life—in other words, a possibility of receiving them. Pure opposing qualities keep matter from receiving a higher form. As those qualities lose their force and opposition, matter becomes more able to receive a higher form. When it is fully prepared for the highest form, its opposing qualities have almost disappeared. It can then receive a perfection like the one received by the matter of the heavens, which is free of opposing forms and qualities: the thinking soul. The highest source is always giving, and once the barrier is gone, matter receives from it.

Near and distant possibilities, then, make matter ready to receive by removing barriers. We have now shown that possibility, potential, and nonexistence do not produce the existence of anything. They prepare the things that can receive existence.

Every thing that comes into being in our world must be preceded by nonexistence. To say that this nonexistence is one of its causes means that matter has shed its earlier form and can now receive a later one. The same applies to things whose nature is to unfold over time, such as time and motion, and whatever depends on them: for each new part to arise, what was already present must pass away. The same is true of continuous things at rest and of mathematical quantities. For one part or point to be present in a place, another must leave it, because these limited things cannot fill the same place all at once.
Chapter 36 — Why powers in bodies need a spatial relation to act

We have established that anything that depends on something else for its existence also depends on it for its actions. This nearly proves the point we are making. Matter exists in space, and anything whose existence depends on matter also depends on a spatial position, at least indirectly. Its power to act depends on that position too. A bodily cause cannot act on something with which it has no spatial relation.

Here is a fuller explanation. Any power that produces an effect works in one of two ways. Either its effect must first occur in a particular place, so that its effects elsewhere depend on what it has already done there; the closer something is to that place, the more readily it receives the effect. Or its action does not depend on first affecting a particular place. Fire is an example of the first kind: its effect varies with distance.
The nearer something is to the fire, the sooner and more strongly it is heated.

When a power's effect depends on a particular body in this way, the power is related to that body either because it needs the body in order to exist, as fire does, or because it needs the body only in order to act, as a soul does. In either case, we can say that it acts through a spatial relation. But a power whose effect depends only on the effect being possible in itself, and whose action is not directed to one body rather than another, has no connection to matter in its existence or in its action. It is wholly independent of bodies and belongs to the realm of immaterial intellects.

This shows that powers in bodies cannot affect the existence or qualities of immaterial beings. Near and far apply only to things that have a place and position. It also follows that bodily powers cannot bring about prime matter or the substantial forms that make a body what it is. So they cannot bring any body into existence.

Someone might object: if a bodily power cannot affect an immaterial being because it has no spatial relation to it, then an immaterial being cannot affect a body either, since it has no spatial relation to bodies. If so, we should not say that immaterial beings bring bodies into existence.

I reply that for an immaterial being to affect something, it is enough that the effect be possible in itself. Once that possibility is present, the effect comes from the immaterial cause, whether or not the effect has a place in space. But for a bodily power to act, the possibility of an effect is not enough. The thing receiving the effect must also have a spatial relation to the body whose power is acting. An immaterial being cannot have that relation to a body.

When matter receives a form or perfection from an immaterial being, matter itself is what receives the effect. It is not merely a channel between the recipient and some other thing. In this case, matter is not the acting cause; it is the recipient. These are two different roles.

You may ask: do philosophers not say that the body's coming into being causes the soul to come into being, even though the soul is immaterial and has no spatial relation to the body? I reply that you will learn how the soul comes to be through the body. Its cause is an immaterial being, while the body carries the possibility of the soul in a certain way, as I will explain later. So the body is a condition that allows the soul to flow from its cause; it does not produce the soul itself.

Likewise, a quality or power that exists in a subject does not cause the subject. It is a condition that lets the subject receive the effects that follow from that quality or power, as I will explain later. A subject and what exists in it have no spatial relation to one another.
Chapter 37 — Why existence alone can act as a cause or be caused

Only existence can act as a cause. Consider anything other than existence apart from its existence: in itself, it stands equally open to existence and nonexistence. So it is not actually existent in itself. Its essence cannot cause anything to exist—not even itself, much less anything else. Whatever causes something must affect that thing's existence. Existence, then, can act as a cause. If we imagined existence apart from essence, it would be even more able to cause things, since essence itself is only possibility and dependence. We already know that what does not exist has no effect. Likewise, if we imagined a material power apart from matter, it would be more able to act because it would be free of matter's defects and limitations. But that is a separate question. Our concern here is that existence can act as a cause in general.

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi raises this objection: existences either differ only in number, or they differ in kind. If they differ only in number, the existence of one thing cannot cause the existence of another. No individual of a single nature has an inherent priority over another; all stand on equal footing. But the other option—that existences differ in kind—cannot be right either. Existence is divided into the existence of substances and the existence of accidents, which exist in something else. The existence of substances is divided into that of bodies and things without bodies; the existence of accidents is divided into the different categories of properties. What is divided must have one meaning in common. The idea of existence is self-evident and shared by all existences; their differences come from features outside that idea. If existences differed in kind, each would be made up of a general kind and a distinguishing feature. Then the existence of the First Effect would be composite, and a single cause would produce more than one effect—a conclusion they reject.

The principles we have already established are enough to set aside arguments like these. We have shown that existence is one simple reality, though it has degrees of strength and weakness, priority and posteriority. Existence can be caused because essences, by themselves, cannot be caused. What can be caused is either existence itself or an essence's being joined to existence. But that joining comes later than the essence and depends on the existence of the essence that receives it, as we have explained. So what is caused in itself is existence alone.

Al-Razi objects that existence is one essence. If so, a cause acting on existence should be able to cause any effect. Here is his argument. When water warms up, warmth is one essence among many. Its actual existence, which flows from separate principles, either depends on a condition or does not. If it does not, warmth must exist forever, since an essence can receive existence and the cause is always giving it. If warmth does depend on a condition, what depends on that condition: the existence of warmth or warmth itself as an essence? The first cannot be right. Contact with water is a condition for coldness, and the existence of coldness is no different from the existence of warmth. So contact with water should also be a condition for the existence of warmth, since whatever is a condition for one thing is a condition for things like it. But then warmth would have to arise whenever water made contact: the essence is ready to receive it, the cause is always giving, and the condition is present. That would mean anything could arise whenever anything else did, with nothing having its own specific cause or condition. Our senses show that this is false.

The second option—that warmth itself, rather than its existence, depends on the condition—leads to the conclusion al-Razi wants. If an essence depends on a condition, it depends on something else. Whatever depends on something else must have a cause, and the chain must eventually end with the Necessary Being. So essences themselves are caused, not just their existence. That is the end of his argument.

I say that the argument fails because it assumes that existence is one essence applied to all things in exactly the same way, rather than a reality that varies in degree. On that assumption, it also follows that God's existence has no effect on anything. Al-Razi has said repeatedly that God's existence is equal to the existence of possible things. Then anything that comes from God's existence could also come from the existence of anything else, so God would have no special power to cause any effect. But a cause must have a particular connection to its effect. Otherwise, its existence would make no more difference than its nonexistence in bringing that effect about. And if its existence makes no difference to whether something comes about, it is not the cause of that thing. God's existence, then, would cause nothing. God is far above such a claim.

Earlier we distinguished between existence as the existence of blackness and blackness as something described as existent. We showed that need cannot belong to existence simply as existence. Need arises only when an essence is considered in relation to its existence: the essence is possible, and so it depends on something else. The essence depends on existence for its being; existence itself is not what depends. As for the claim that essences are not caused, we have already explained how to understand it.

Al-Razi and those who think like him assume that an effect must first have its own identity before the cause acts on it. Only then, they think, does it acquire a need that is not part of its essence, and the cause gives it existence. They think this applies to essences, since an essence relates to existence like a receiver to what it receives, or like matter to form when we consider them separately. So they conclude that a cause produces an essence's being existent, not existence itself. But they have missed this: without existence, how could an essence arise at all and then be possible, dependent, necessary, and finally existent? We have explained how an essence is described in these ways, so there is no need to repeat it. We have also explained how existences themselves depend on the giver of existence even more deeply than essences do, and what it means for existence itself to come to be through dependence on its cause.

When al-Razi says that essences are not caused, he means that being caused is not part of what an essence means. This is like saying that an essence's attributes do not belong to it when we consider it just as it is in itself. That means only that the attribute does not belong to it under that description; it does not mean that the attribute never belongs to it in reality. In the same way, essences are caused in the sense that being caused truly applies to them, though they are not caused in the sense that being caused is part of their essence.
This is what al-Razi means by his reinterpretation. Our approach has shown that the first of these two senses leads to the second.
Chapter 38 — Why an effect need not be preceded by nonexistence

This question is like the one in the previous chapter. It belongs in a discussion of cause and effect, but it also fits with what we will say about what comes before and after. Since some debaters have taken a strong stand against this view, we need to make the case more firmly. I will give several proofs.

First, the universe is either possible in itself at all times, or its possibility is not eternal. The second option is impossible. If its possibility were not eternal, the universe would have to be impossible in itself: it cannot be necessary in itself, and what is impossible in itself cannot become possible. Its becoming possible must be due either to what it is or to something outside it. If it is due to what it is, then its possibility always held. If it is due to something outside it, that cause is either eternal or not. If it is eternal, the impossibility it brought about could never end. If it is not eternal, we must ask the same question about that cause. This line of reasoning must eventually reach something necessary in itself, and then the impossibility could never end.

Someone may object: even if this impossibility depends on the Necessary Being, its effect may depend on a condition. When that condition disappears, so does the effect. I reply that if the condition is necessary in itself, it cannot disappear, so the impossibility cannot disappear either. If the condition is not necessary in itself, we must ask the same question about it. The reasoning does not go on without end; it ends with something that exists necessarily in itself. So we cannot claim that possible things were unable to exist from eternity.

But there is a difficulty. If we consider an event as something preceded by nonexistence, then its possibility cannot be limited to one time rather than another, given the arguments above. Its possibility must always hold. Yet that does not mean the event stops being an event. We have taken it as something preceded by nonexistence, and being preceded by nonexistence is part of what it is. That feature cannot be removed. If the event can be possible at all times and still remain an event, this proof does not hold.

I reply that we are not discussing things whose very nature is change and coming-to-be. We are discussing things whose nature can have coming-to-be as a feature. Many things, such as parts of motion and time, cannot last forever; they necessarily come into being. They need a cause because they are possible, but their possibility is only the possibility of this kind of existence: lasting existence is impossible for them. A thing's being possible means that some kind of existence is open to it, not that every kind of existence is open to it. A substance cannot exist as an attribute, just as blackness cannot be whiteness. Motion and things like it cannot exist by lasting unchanged.

Here is a second proof. If an effect needs a prior nonexistence, it must be either because the effect itself needs that nonexistence in order to exist, or because the agent needs it in order to act. The first is impossible. If the effect needed nonexistence in order to exist, that nonexistence would have to be present along with it. But nonexistence at the same time as the effect contradicts the effect. Something that contradicts an effect cannot be a condition for it. The second is impossible too. The effect's existence contradicts its nonexistence, and a condition that contradicts what it must accompany cannot be a condition at all. So neither an effect's existence nor an agent's power to act requires a prior nonexistence.

Here is another proof. When events come into being and continue to exist, they either need a cause while they exist or they do not. If they do, they need a cause from eternity to eternity, because they remain possible in themselves. If they do not, then either they have ceased to be possible, or they have remained possible but no longer need a cause. They cannot have ceased to be possible: what is possible in itself cannot become necessary in itself. And if possibility belongs to a thing by its own nature, it is always possible. If possibility comes from something outside it, then the fact that it is possible must also be possible. That would require another possibility, and that one yet another, leading to an endless chain. So events remain possible while they continue to exist, and therefore still need a cause, because possibility is the basis of that need.

Someone may ask: once a thing exists, does it not become more likely to exist than not? This greater likelihood either belongs to existence itself or is an added feature. If it belongs to existence itself, then as soon as something exists, this greater likelihood is present; once present, it makes the thing independent of a cause. But the cause is needed for the thing to exist. Its existence would then remove its own cause, which is impossible. If the greater likelihood is an added feature, it must have a cause. The thing depends on that feature, and the feature depends on a cause, so the thing is not independent of a cause.

Here is another proof. An effect might be said to need a cause because it exists now, because it was once nonexistent, or because its existence was preceded by nonexistence. It cannot need a cause because of nonexistence itself, since nonexistence is nothing and needs no cause. Nor can it need a cause because its existence was preceded by nonexistence. Being preceded by nonexistence is a feature that necessarily belongs to the event once it exists. A thing may be possible in itself, yet a feature that belongs to it can be necessary: four can be possible, while being even is necessary for it. In the same way, an event may be possible, while having come after nonexistence is necessary for it. What needs a cause, then, is existence alone.

Here is another proof. God has attributes and features that follow from Him. Different schools understand them in different ways: as relations or negative descriptions, as positive realities, or as states and forms within divine knowledge. None of these attributes is necessary in itself, since there cannot be more than one Necessary Being. They are possible in themselves but necessarily belong to God. So a cause can produce an effect without that effect first having been nonexistent.

Someone might reply that these attributes are not acts, and that only acts need to be preceded by nonexistence. I answer: even if we agree that something not preceded by nonexistence should not be called an act, we have shown that something possible in itself can depend on a cause that exists eternally alongside it. Once this is accepted, there is no reason to forbid it in some cases. The only remaining objection would be to the word “act,” and that has no value in an argument about reality.

Here is another proof. Features that belong to a thing by its nature depend on it, but do not come after it in time. Features that follow existence also never leave it. There is no time when four is not even, a triangle does not have three angles, or fire is not hot. We can go further: a cause and its effect can exist together. Heating and burning happen together; pain follows a harmful imbalance or a separation in the body. A clearer example is that knowledge gives rise to being knowledgeable, and power gives rise to being able. These effects exist along with their causes; they do not wait until later. So a cause and its effect being present at the same time does not remove the effect's dependence on the cause.

Here is another proof. A thing, considered as existing, must exist; considered as absent, it must be absent. This is a kind of necessity that follows from the condition we set. Coming into being is the order of these two states. If we consider a thing only under these conditions, its existence and its nonexistence are both necessary in their respective states. Necessity leaves no room for dependence on a cause. So coming into being, considered just as coming into being, cannot be what makes a thing need a cause. If we do not consider the thing only under those conditions, it still has necessary existence while it exists and necessary nonexistence while it is absent. But considered in itself, it still needs a cause. We can see, then, that what makes a thing need a cause is its possibility, not its coming into being.

Here is another proof. The basis of a thing's dependence must not remain unchanged when its cause is present. Otherwise, it would still need another cause. But coming into being remains true of an event whether or not its cause is present. If coming into being were what made the event need a cause, the problem would remain. If possibility is the basis of its need, however, it does not remain unchanged once the cause is present: the essence, as an effect of that cause, becomes necessary. So possibility, and nothing else, is what makes a thing need a cause.

These are ten proofs that a possible essence needs a cause because it is possible. A caused existence itself depends on its giver by its very nature, not because of some added feature. Even so, we have also proved that the whole universe and everything in it came into being in time. I will return to this, if God wills.

Those who reject this principle offer weak arguments. First, bringing about what already exists is impossible, so the need for a cause must come before existence. Second, if two things have both existed from eternity, neither has a better claim than the other to depend on its companion, since neither has an advantage over the other. Third, it is established that the Creator of the universe acts by choice. But choice and intention apply only to bringing something into being; we find that we cannot intend to create something that already exists. Fourth, once a building exists, it no longer needs a builder; once writing exists, it no longer needs a writer.

The first argument can be answered in two ways. We can challenge it by pointing out that being able requires power, and being black requires blackness, among other examples. Or we can answer it directly: bringing about something that already exists is not impossible; in some cases it is necessary. What is impossible is giving existence a second time to something that already exists. Besides, the argument assumes the very point it is meant to prove.

The second argument fails because a cause is not a cause simply because it has existed from eternity. Nor is an effect an effect simply because it came into being in time. That would make neither of two things that came into being more fit to cause the other—for example, the motion of a hand and the motion of a key it turns. A cause is a cause because of what it is. Its very nature gives it priority over its effect, as the sun is prior to its light: light comes from the sun, not the other way around. The related objection—that if two things are inseparable, the absence of either must mean the absence of the other, so neither has more claim to be the cause—has already been answered.

As for the third argument, choice and intention bring about the beginning of an action, while their continuation goes with the action's continuation. If intention and choice continue, they can continue to direct an action as well. To claim this is impossible simply assumes what is in question.

As for the fourth argument, builders and writers cause bodies to move and change place. They are not the causes that preserve a building's shape, keep things in place, or make them last. Other, nearer or more distant causes do that. I will explain this in its proper place.
Chapter 39 — Why every event in time depends on an unbroken circular motion

Know that a complete cause cannot come before or after its effect in time. So the immediate causes of events must themselves come into being. If they had always existed, their effects would have always existed too. Whenever a cause exists while its effect does not, the effect is possible in relation to that cause: what is impossible in itself cannot be produced by a cause. So when the effect does come into being, something else must tip the balance toward its existence rather than its nonexistence. That something also needs a cause, and the same question arises again, until we reach what makes the effect necessary and brings it into being.

The immediate cause of an event, or at least one part of its cause, must therefore come into being along with it. We can ask the same question about that new cause. This leads either to an endless chain or to an event whose very nature is to change and come into being, such as motion, or a nature that renews itself. But a nature that comes and goes, whose absence belongs to an earlier time and motion, must be preceded by another nature that keeps its time. This time-keeping nature has two sides. One is known to God: His eternal knowledge and the form of His decree, which is not part of the created world. The other belongs to the created world and comes into being anew each day.

The philosophers accepted an endless chain because they had not found this principle. They said the chain must either exist all at once or be arranged so that one thing comes before another. The first option is impossible, as we have already shown, so they chose the second. But then the events in the chain must either be separate instants or unfold over time. If they are separate instants, they must follow one another without end. That is impossible. And even if it were possible, each instant would be separate from the next, so the earlier instant would not have to end in the later one. It could not be the cause of the later instant, contrary to what they assumed. If the events unfold over time, they are motion.

Here is the point. When something new arises in matter—for example, a human form in semen—the cause gains a relation to that matter that it did not have before. The matter must move and change so that what was far from receiving the form comes closer. The semen undergoes a connected series of changes. Its powers and conditions shift until it becomes suited to receive that form from its active cause.

To explain this, a cause may either prepare something or bring about its effect. A preparing cause may come before the effect because it does not produce the effect itself. It only brings the recipient close to the point where the acting cause can produce it. The acting cause, by contrast, must be present with its effect. Preparation consists of a real process of change, linked step by step: each new state can arise only after the previous one has passed away.

Consider a heavy body falling. It does not reach any point along its path without becoming ready to move from there to the next point. Reaching each point prepares it for the next part of its fall. Its weight is what moves it. But until the body has reached a given point, its weight cannot move it from there. Once it reaches that point, its weight can move it onward. The earlier motion brings the body closer to the next effect; this is what philosophers mean when they say that motion brings causes closer to their effects.

The same thing happens when someone walks through a dark place by the light of a lamp. As the person steps onto a patch of ground lit by the lamp, the light falls on the next patch, which the person can then reach. The lamp directly causes the light on each patch; walking prepares the next patch to be reached. Likewise, someone who intends to make a pilgrimage has one general aim that gives rise to a sequence of smaller intentions. Reaching each point along the way makes it possible to form the next intention and move toward the next point. The general aim causes these smaller intentions and the movements that follow them, and remains present throughout.
